parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek αγάλι(α) (agáli(a), “slowly, gradually”).
From Greek αλλα φράνκα (alla fránka). The first component (ала- (ala-)) is analyzable as ала́ (alá). The noun sense is a nominalization of the adjective and/or adverb senses.

From Greek βάλσαμο (válsamo) or Italian balsamo. Attributed by RBE to Phoenician, but with no etymon given; the corresponding Ancient Greek etymon does not appear to be derived from Phoenician but from Hebrew בָּשָׂם.

parole.significato: marching band, wind ensemble (group of instrumental musicians in woodwind and brass families who generally perform outd…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μπάντα (bánta) and Italian banda, apparently from German Bande.
Borrowed from Greek μπαράκα (baráka) or Turkish baraka, from Italian baracca. First attested in 1855.
Borrowed from Greek μπαστούνι (bastoúni), from Italian bastone.
Borrowed from Greek μπόλι (bóli).

parole.significato: to dye, to paint, to colour (to colour or cover something with dye or paint)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek βἀπτω (vapto).

parole.significato: to fight with, to contend with, to be in discord with
parole.testo: Disputed: * Per Bulgarian Etymological Dictionary, reanalyzed from Greek βιάζω (viázo, “to force”); * Per Meljničuk (in discussion of Ukrainian васнь (vasnʹ)), possibly related to Proto-Slavic *vasnь (“feud”).

parole.significato: geology (the science that studies the structure of the Earth (or other planets), together with its origin and developme…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Greek γεωλογία (geología), from γῆ (gí, “earth”) + -λογία (-logía, “study”). By surface analysis, гео- (geo-) + -логия (-logija).

parole.significato: gyro (style of Greek sandwich commonly filled with grilled meat, tomato, onions, and tzatziki sauce)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek γύρος (gýros).
Borrowed from Greek γλάρος (gláros, “gull”).
Derived from Greek δυόσμος (dyósmos, “mint, spearmint”), from Ancient Greek ἡδύοσμον (hēdúosmon, “green mint”).
Borrowed from Greek δισάκι (disáki, “double sacks”). Root akin to French loanword Bulgarian сак (sak, “sack”), ultimately from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos).

Borrowed from Greek ζάχαρη (záchari), borrowed from Byzantine Greek ζάχαρις (zákharis), from Ancient Greek σάκχαρις (sákkharis), from σάκχαρ (sákkhar), borrowed from Pali sakkharā, from Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Eu

parole.significato: icon (type of religious painting portraying a saint or scene from Scripture, often done on wooden panels)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek εικόνα (eikóna), from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn).

parole.significato: pupa (metamorphic stage of development in insects, between larva and imago)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek κακαβίδα (kakavída, “pupa”).
Borrowed from Greek καμάρα (kamára, “vault, arch”). Also borrowed, with the same meaning, into Serbo-Croatian кȁмара.
Borrowed from Greek καμπάνα (kampána), borrowed from Italian campana.
Borrowed from Greek κανέλλα (kanélla), from Italian cannella.

parole.significato: hat (first attested in the 14th century, but in common usage only as of the 17th century in Kostur)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek κάπα (kápa). Cognate with Bulgarian ша́пка (šápka) and Bulgarian капе́ла (kapéla).

parole.significato: carbine (weapon similar to a rifle but much shorter in length)
parole.testo: Borrowed through Greek καραμπίνα (karampína), Italian carabina or Turkish karabina, from French carabine. First attested in 1853.
Borrowed from Greek καρδάρα (kardára), derived καρδάρι (kardári) + -α (-a) but reanalyzed as from -άρα (-ára) in Bulgarian, from Byzantine Greek καλδάριον (kaldárion), from Latin caldārium.

parole.significato: pin (needle without an eye, used for fastening)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek καρφίτσα (karfítsa, “pin”), a diminutive of καρφί (karfí, “nail; rivet”). Compare Turkish karfiçe, Albanian karficë and Aromanian cãrfițã.

Borrowed from Greek κέφαλος (kéfalos, “mullet; gray mullet”), from Ancient Greek κέφᾰλος (képhălos, “grey mullet”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰébʰōl (“head”). Cognates include Turkish kefal, Russian кефа́ль (kefálʹ), Albanian qefull and Romanian chefal.
Borrowed from Greek κόκαλο (kókalo), κόκκαλο (kókkalo).
Borrowed from Greek κόλλα (kólla, “sheet (of paper)”).
Borrowed from Greek κόλλυβον (kóllyvon).

Borrowed from Greek κομμάτι (kommáti, “piece”), from Ancient Greek κομμάτιον (kommátion) - a diminutive of κόμμα (kómma, “piece”), which also gives English comma. Cognates include Serbo-Croatian комад, Slovene komad and Aromanian cumatã.

Borrowed from Greek κρεβάτι (kreváti), probably ultimately from Ancient Macedonian *γράβος (grabos, “oak”). If correct, then related to native Bulgarian га́бър (gábăr, “hornbeam”) (reanalyzed from an earlier *grabrъ).
Onomatopoeic derivative of the call of the cuckoo. In some dialects, it's borrowed from Greek κούκος (koúkos), κούκκος (koúkkos).
Borrowed from Greek κουμαριά (koumariá, “strawberry tree”) or Greek κούμαρο (koúmaro, “strawberry tree fruit”) with -ка (-ka, “feminine noun forming suffix”).

parole.significato: bowl (container used to hold, mix or present food)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek κούπα (koúpa), from Late Latin cuppa, from Latin cūpa. Cognate with English cup.
Borrowed from Greek λαβράκι (lavráki), from Ancient Greek λάβραξ (lábrax).

parole.significato: any member of the species (Rumex) of edible dock, in particular patience dock (Rumex patientia). Derived terms sometime…
parole.testo: Hypercorrect spelling of ла́пат (lápat) with word-final consonant voicing. Borrowed from Greek λάπατο (lápato, “sorrel”), from Ancient Greek λάπαθον (lápathon). Further etymology uncertain. Cognate with Albanian lëpjetë, Portuguese labaça and Italian lapazio, among others.
From Greek λέντιον (léntion), itself from Latin linteum (linen cloth). Cf. Serbo-Croatian лента / lenta (silken belt).
Borrowed from Greek λιβάδι (livádi).

Borrowed from Greek λεμονάδα (lemonáda), from Venetan łimonada. First attested in 1846. The form with -адь (-adʹ) is borrowed from Russian лимонад (limonad), and the one with -ата (-ata) arose by influence of either Ottoman Turkish لیموناطه (limonata) or Italian limonata. Cognates include Serbo-Croa
Borrowed from Greek μαγεία (mageía), and, as an internationalism, via French magie, German Magie, Polish magia and Russian ма́гия (mágija).
Borrowed from Greek μαγνήτης (magnítis).

parole.significato: master (someone who has mastered a field of specialty)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μάστορας (mástoras).
Borrowed from Greek μακάρι (makári).

parole.significato: dairy farm (place where dairy farming is practiced and dairy cattle is held)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μάντρα (mántra).
Borrowed from Greek μαρούλια pl (maroúlia).

parole.significato: mastic, mastika (a strong alcoholic drink flavoured with anise or mastic, common in Bulgaria and the Balkans)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μαστίχα (mastícha, “mastic, mastic resin; mastic-flavoured drink”), ultimately from μαστίχη (mastíchi, “mastic resin”).
Borrowed from Greek μύδια (mýdia), plural of μύδι (mýdi, “mussel”).
Borrowed from Greek μύρισμα (mýrisma).

parole.significato: to smell (to have a particular smell)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μυρίζω (myrízo).
Borrowed from Greek μολύβι (molývi, “pencil”). Compare Albanian molivë and Aromanian muliv.

parole.significato: you (general vocative expression, used to augment an address)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μωρέ (moré), frozen vocative of μωρός (morós), meaning “stupid”, but commonly used as a colloquial address.
Borrowed from Greek μούχλα (moúchla).
Borrowed from Greek μουτσούνα (moutsoúna), derived from Italian muso. Akin to English muzzle (a French borrowing).

Borrowed from Greek χοχλίας (chochlías), a dialectal variation of Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías, “snail”) (whence Old Church Slavonic кохль (koxlĭ), Latin cōchlea (“snail”)). Originally referring to the spiral shell of the snail, later generalized to mean the whole animal.
Borrowed from Greek πανηγύρι (panigýri). Compare Macedonian панаѓур (panaǵur).

parole.significato: parrot (tropical bird of family Psittacidae, native to Africa and America)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek παπαγάλος (papagálos), of Arabic origin (see Arabic بَبَّغَاء (babbaḡāʔ)). Akin to the outdated English popinjay.

parole.significato: chapel (Christian place of prayer and worship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek παρεκκλήσι (parekklísi).

Ultimately from Greek παγούρι (pagoúri, “flask”); however, in view of the attested variants, more likely borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پاغوریه (pağuri) (where Turkish -ğ- can be reflected as -х-, -в-, -г- or -∅- in Bulgarian).

parole.significato: pendant (a coin, a piece of jewellery or another decoration worn on a necklace)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πεντάρα (pentára, “five-cent coin”).
Borrowed from Greek περούκα (peroúka) or French perruque.

parole.significato: pepper (a vegetable plant with a hollow fleshy fruit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πιπέρι (pipéri).
Borrowed from Greek πίτα (píta, “pie”), of unclear further origin. Doublet of пи́ца (píca) (Italian borrowing).

parole.significato: jelly (broth made of glazed egg albumen and gelatin)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πηχτή (pichtí, “brawn”).
Via Greek πόρτα (pórta), Byzantine Greek πόρτα (pórta) from Latin porta. Compare Old Church Slavonic поръта (porŭta) from the same source.
Borrowed from Greek πορτοκάλι (portokáli) and/or Ottoman Turkish پورتقال (portokal). Ultimately from Italian portogallo.

parole.significato: leek (type of onion with a long cylindrical stem, white to light green long layered leaves and with a slightly spicy ta…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πράσο (práso).

parole.significato: oregano (herb of genus Origanum, within the Lamiaceae family)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek ρίγανη (rígani), ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀρῑ́γᾰνον (orī́gănon). Doublet of орига́но (origáno).
Borrowed from Greek σαλαμούρα (salamoúra).

parole.significato: salad (vegetables cut into pieces; or, rarely, meat or fruit, with added spices)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek σαλάτα (saláta).
Borrowed from Greek σαμάρι (samári).

parole.significato: satrap (a governor of a province in ancient Persia)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek σατράπης (satrápis, “governor”), from Ancient Greek σατράπης (satrápēs), ultimately from Old Median *xšaθrapāwan- (literally “kingdom-protector”).

parole.significato: jack mackerel, Mediterranean horse mackerel (Trachurus mediterraneus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek σαφρίδι (safrídi), from Byzantine Greek σαυρίδιον (saurídion), from Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros). See the latter for further etymology.
Borrowed from Greek σινάπι (sinápi).
From Greek ἐσχάρα (eschára) (see also related Greek σχάρα (schára))
Borrowed from Greek γαρίδα (garída).

parole.significato: cardueline finch (passerine bird of genus Carduelis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek σκαθί (skathí), σκαρθί (skarthí, “siskin”), borrowed also in Romanian scatiu (“siskin”), Turkish iskete (“titmouse”).
Borrowed from Greek σκουμπρί (skoumprí).
Borrowed from Greek σπαθί (spathí). Via its Proto-Indo-European reconstruction, cognate with English spade.

Probably borrowed from Greek σπήλαιο (spílaio, “cavern”) with semantic shift. Identical with Macedonian спила (spila, “cliff”) and also loaned into Serbo-Croatian спи̏ља/шпи̏ља (“cave”), Aromanian spilă (“cave”). Formally resembles Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp point, spike”) (compare English s
Borrowed from Greek στρείδι (streídi).
Borrowed from Greek έταιριασα (étairiasa).

parole.significato: frying pan, pan (round metal shallow cooking pan with a long handle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek τηγάνι (tigáni).

parole.significato: dining room (A room in a dwelling intended for eating.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek τραπεζαρία (trapezaría).
Borrowed from Greek τριαντάφυλλο (triantáfyllo).

parole.significato: a triangular pastry made of puff pastry, typically filled with nuts or cream and soaked in sugar syrup
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek τρίγωνο (trígono).
Modelled after Greek πριόνι (prióni, “saw”), with root reanalysed to resemble native три́я (tríja, “to rub, to scratch”).
Borrowed from Greek φάρος (fáros, “beacon”).
Borrowed from Greek φασούλι (fasoúli), from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos), ultimately from Latin phaseolus. Cognate with Turkish fasulye.

parole.significato: frappé (Greek iced coffee drink generally made from spray-dried instant coffee, water, sugar, and milk)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek φραπέ (frapé), borrowed from French frappé.
Borrowed from Greek φουστάνι (foustáni), of Venetan origin.

parole.significato: halloumi (a traditional cheese from Cyprus, made from goat's and/or sheep's milk)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek χαλλούμι (challoúmi).

parole.significato: to like, to have a liking for
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek αρέσω (aréso).
Borrowed from Greek χιλιάδα (chiliáda). First attested in the 14th century.
Borrowed from Greek χορός (chorós).

parole.significato: to tell, to say, to state
parole.testo: Rebracketing of an earlier хоратя́ (horatjá) + -увам (-uvam), from Greek χωρατεύω (choratévo, “to bring together, to communicate”).
Borrowed from Greek κρύωμα (krýoma, “cold”).
Borrowed from Greek σέλινο (sélino), along with Romanian țelină.

parole.significato: infecund, not succeeding in getting children
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek στείρος (steíros).
